The two-year property tax cycle

Arkansas works on a two-year rhythm. Values and millage rates are fixed in the assessment year, and the money is collected the year after. The state Department of Finance and Administration oversees all 75 counties, but assessing, collecting and distributing are local jobs.

During the assessment year, county assessors, clerks, equalization boards and judges settle values. School boards, city councils and county quorum courts set millage, and the quorum court formally levies it. During the collection year, county clerks, collectors and treasurers send bills, take payments and pass the money along. Each assessment year doubles as the collection year for the year before, so an owner is always living in two cycles at once.

Business personal property is assessed by May 31. Homeowners care mostly about the notice in summer, the hearing windows in late summer and fall, and the October 15 due date.

What millage rate will a house pay?

Across counties the state average is 48.80 mills, built from school, city and county rates set after the 2025 school elections. By layer that is 38.52 for schools, 4.17 for cities and 7.93 for counties.

Assessed value is 20% of market value, and millage is applied to that assessed figure. Schools receive about 80% of collections, counties about 15% and cities about 5%. Your own rate depends on the school district, city and county the house sits in, so two homes of equal value can get different bills. Read the assessor's notice for the actual millage on your parcel.

Reappraisal and assessment caps

Counties reappraise every four years under Act 139 of 2023, and by 2028 every county will be on a four-year contract. Ask your assessor when your county's next reappraisal lands, since a reappraisal is when values jump.

Under Amendment 79, the taxable value of a homestead owned by someone under 65 who is not disabled can rise only 5% a year after a reappraisal. Other real property is capped at 10% a year. Credits for homesteads and the age 65 or disabled freeze are covered in the homestead guide, so this page stays with assessment and collection.

A cap slows the climb of the taxable figure. It cannot stop a bill from growing when a school board raises millage.

Dates every Arkansas owner should know

The calendar below blends the statewide schedule with how Pulaski County runs its equalization process, which shows how one county applies the rules.

DateWhat happens
JulyAssessor mails notices of assessed value (Pulaski County)
August 1Equalization board holds its organizational meeting (Pulaski County)
Third Monday in AugustLast day to schedule a board hearing

Second Monday in OctoberLast day to petition county court
October 15Taxes due; unpaid bills turn delinquent
November 15County court must hear and rule on appeals
First business day of MarchCollection of the prior assessment year's bills begins

No assessment can be changed after the board's special session ends in November, so an owner who misses the August deadline should not expect a second chance that year.

How to appeal your assessment

The path runs from a conversation with the county assessor, to the county equalization board, to county court, and then to circuit court. The appeal statute, 26-27-318, controls the county court step.

  • The board hears only the current year's value and cannot take appeals of earlier years.
  • A county court petition goes to the county clerk, who assigns a case number. There is no filing fee.
  • You must have gone to the board first, unless you never received the required notice of a value change.
  • The county court has to publish notice at least a week before the hearing, or it lacks jurisdiction.
  • You carry the burden of proving true value by a preponderance of the evidence, and no presumption favors the assessor.
  • The court's written decision is due within 20 working days after the hearing and must tell you that you can go on to circuit court.

Many values change after informal talks alone, so the first conversation with the assessor is worth having. Before heading to circuit court, ask an attorney about the deadline.

When taxes go unpaid

Taxes unpaid after October 15 are delinquent and carry a 10% penalty plus daily interest on real estate. The collector publishes delinquent lists in a local newspaper.

The county does not hold a sale. Under Ark. Code 26-37-101, land still unpaid a year after the due date is certified to the Commissioner of State Lands by July 1 of the following year, and title vests in the state when certification arrives. The tax deed guide walks through what follows.

If you plan to sell, treat a delinquent bill as urgent rather than something to settle quietly later. After certification, the payoff goes through the state's office and the redemption deadline is firm.

The tax lien and who pays at a sale

The property tax lien arises on the first Monday of January of the year of assessment and lasts until the tax and penalties are paid. Section 26-34-101 ranks it ahead of judgments, executions, encumbrances and other liens, whenever those were created.

Between a grantor and a grantee, the statute holds the lien back until the last date set by law for the county clerk to deliver the tax books to the collector. That timing is why the tax bill is a closing item and not just the seller's private matter.

Collection runs from the first business day of March through October 15 of the year after assessment. A house sold in spring can close while the prior year's bill is unpaid. The title company can ask the collector for a status and pay what is owed from the seller's proceeds.

Selling with taxes owed

Before listing, confirm three things with the county: what you owe, what the next assessment will do, and whether any year is already delinquent.

  • Ask the collector for the current balance, with penalty and interest, by parcel number.
  • Read the latest assessor notice and see whether your county is reappraising this year.
  • If the August hearing date is behind you, calendar the second Monday in October for county court.
  • If a year is delinquent, find out whether it has been certified to the Commissioner of State Lands.

Cash Home Buyers makes as-is offers on Arkansas houses, including houses with back taxes. Bring your latest tax statement and assessor notice, and the title company can pay the collector at closing.

Frequently asked questions

When is Arkansas property tax due?

Taxes are collected from the first business day of March through October 15 of the year after assessment. A payment after October 15 draws a 10% penalty, and delinquent real estate accrues interest daily.

What is the deadline to challenge my assessment?

Schedule an equalization board hearing by the third Monday in August. If you disagree with the board, file a county court petition by the second Monday in October. The board cannot hear earlier years.

Does it cost anything to appeal to county court?

No filing fee applies to the petition of appeal under 26-27-318. File with the county clerk, who assigns a case number, and the county court must rule by November 15.

How much can my homestead value rise in one year?

After a reappraisal, taxable value on a homestead owned by someone under 65 who is not disabled can rise 5% a year. Other real property is capped at 10% a year under Amendment 79.

Who sets my millage rate?

School boards, city councils and county quorum courts set it during the assessment year, and the quorum court formally levies it. The statewide county average is 48.80 mills.

What the credit is worth

An Arkansas homeowner can take up to $675 a year off the property tax bill on a qualifying home. House Bill 1103 of 2026 raised the figure from $600. Because older numbers still circulate, call your county assessor to confirm the amount before you quote it to a buyer or a tax preparer.

People say exemption, but what Arkansas provides is a credit. Amendment 79, section 3, directs the General Assembly to give an annual state credit against property tax on a homestead, and the credit can never exceed the tax owed. Picture a $650 bill: the credit wipes out $650 and the state does not mail you the difference.

Who qualifies and where to apply

The house must be your principal place of residence, and you must hold a qualifying ownership interest. File with the assessor's office in the county where the house sits.

  • Record owners qualify, as do buyers under a recorded sales contract and people holding a recorded life estate.
  • A home held in a revocable or irrevocable trust can qualify.
  • Someone who deeded the home away but kept a recorded life estate and still lives there can qualify.
  • A nursing home or retirement center resident who still owns the residence may qualify in some circumstances.
  • An LLC can qualify with a certificate of good standing and an attestation, signed by a member, that the house is that member's primary residence and no other credit is claimed.

Each owner gets one homestead credit per year. A rental, a vacant inherited house and a second home all fail the principal residence test.

Other property tax relief

Amendment 79 created three more tools alongside the credit: a freeze for owners 65 and older or disabled, a 5% yearly cap on homestead increases, and a 10% cap on other real property. Here is how the four compare.

ReliefWho gets itEffect on the taxHow to claim
Homestead creditOwner-occupantsUp to $675 off the yearly billApply with the county assessor
Age 65 or disabled freezeHomestead owners who qualify for the creditFreezes the taxable assessed valueApply with the county assessor
Homestead capHomesteads after a reappraisalTaxable value climbs 5% a year until it reaches full assessed valueBuilt into the assessment
Cap on other real propertyCommercial, agricultural and vacant parcelsTaxable value climbs 10% a year until full valueBuilt into the assessment

New construction, newly discovered property and substantial improvements fall outside the caps. A substantial improvement is renovation, reconstruction or refurbishment that adds 25% or more to the property's value.

Applying step by step

Start at the assessor's office for the county where the house sits. Confirm that you live there as your principal residence and tell the clerk how you hold title: as record owner, under a recorded sales contract, as a life tenant, through a trust or through an LLC. Trust and LLC owners should expect to hand over extra paperwork, such as the good standing certificate and member attestation described above.

If you are 65 or older or disabled, ask about the freeze in the same visit and bring the proof listed in the next section. Ask what the filing window is for your county, and keep a copy of whatever you submit. A buyer or title company may later ask for it when the property is sold or refinanced.

How the age 65 or disabled freeze works

The freeze locks the home's taxable assessed value at the next assessment date after you turn 65 or become disabled. The tax bill itself is not locked. If a city, county or school district raises its millage, you still pay more.

Someone who is already 65 or disabled when they buy can have the value frozen at the next assessment date after the purchase. You must apply. Bring proof: a driver's license, state ID or birth certificate for age, or a Medicare card or Social Security award letter for disability.

Adding onto the house can end the freeze. The assessor removes it after an addition and you reapply at the new value.

What happens to the credit and the freeze when you sell?

Neither one goes with the house. A freeze cannot pass to the next owner of the same home, and a buyer cannot step into the seller's earlier limit.

Ark. Code § 26-26-1123 controls. After a sale, the assessor values the property at 20% of its appraised value on the next assessment date following the transfer of title. The new owner cannot claim an assessment limit until the second assessment date after the transfer. That is why a buyer's first bill can look much higher than yours did.

As the seller, do these three things:

  • Tell the assessor when the house stops being your principal residence.
  • Do not count on a second credit. If you buy another home, the one-credit-per-year rule still applies.
  • Decide in the contract who pays the bill that arrives after closing. Arkansas bills a year behind, so the 2026 assessment is billed in spring 2027 and due October 15, 2027.
Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Arkansas houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Homestead tax credit versus creditor protection

The tax credit trims a property tax bill. Shielding a homestead from judgment creditors is a different subject, handled under Article 9 of the Arkansas Constitution.

Article 9, section 3 protects the homestead of a resident who is married or the head of a family from a judgment lien and from sale under execution, with exceptions the constitution lists. How that plays out for a given house, including in bankruptcy, needs a lawyer's reading. Filing for the tax credit neither creates nor removes that protection.

Selling with taxes owed

The credit ends with your ownership, and a cash price does not change that. What matters at sale time is the paperwork and any unpaid balance.

Property taxes are due to the county collector by October 15 each year. Unpaid balances after that date draw a 10% penalty, and real estate taxes also pick up 10% annual interest. Parcels that stay delinquent are certified to the Commissioner of State Lands, and title vests in the state. If you are behind, pay the balance before you list or sign a contract.

Expect these steps at a typical closing:

  • Ask the collector for a payoff figure by parcel number.
  • Have the title company pay any balance out of your proceeds.
  • Buy the transfer stamp for the deed.
  • Send the assessor a note that the property changed hands.

The deed carries its own tax. The real property transfer tax is $3.30 per $1,000 of consideration on transactions above $100, paid with a stamp on the deed. A cash sale skips the lender's appraisal and repair demands, but it does not skip these tax items.

Frequently asked questions

Does Arkansas have a homestead exemption?

Arkansas gives a homestead property tax credit, not an exemption of value. It is worth up to $675 a year on a principal residence, and owners 65 or older or disabled can also apply to freeze the taxable assessed value.

Where do I apply for the Arkansas homestead credit?

Apply at the assessor's office in the county where the home sits. That office also handles the age 65 and disability freeze, so ask it for the form and the filing window.

Does the buyer inherit my homestead credit when I sell?

No. The buyer applies as a new owner. Under Ark. Code § 26-26-1123 the buyer gets no assessment limit until the second assessment date after the transfer, and a freeze cannot pass on.

Can I claim the credit on a rental or second home?

No. Only a homestead used as the owner's principal residence qualifies, and each owner can claim one credit per year.

Will turning 65 stop my property taxes from rising?

No. The freeze holds the taxable assessed value, not the bill. If a city, county or school district raises millage, your taxes can still go up.

Arkansas estate tax

Arkansas doesn't have one anymore. Act 645 of 2003 ended it, and anyone who died after December 31, 2004 leaves behind no state estate tax return.

That answers the first question most heirs ask. Arkansas takes no cut of the estate because of its size, and there is no state form to prepare for it. The Department of Finance and Administration publishes a one-page notice about the repeal. Print it for the probate file in case a title company or lender wants proof.

The notice speaks only to the estate tax. If the inheritance is large, run the details past a probate attorney before you distribute anything.

Federal estate tax

The federal tax applies to a small slice of estates. A return is due only if the gross estate, added to adjusted taxable gifts and the specific gift tax exemption, tops the filing threshold for the year of death. For a 2026 death that threshold is $15,000,000.

Plain, modest estates seldom need to file. When one does, the gross estate is counted at its fair market value on the date of death. Deductions can include mortgages and other debts, administration expenses, anything passing to a surviving spouse and gifts to qualified charities. A surviving spouse can also elect portability on a timely filed return, which carries over the decedent's unused exemption.

Year of deathFederal filing thresholdArkansas estate tax return
2023$12,920,000None required
2024$13,610,000None required
2025$13,990,000None required
2026$15,000,000None required

Income tax when an heir sells

Usually the bill is small, because an heir's tax basis starts at the home's worth on the day the owner died. Under Publication 551, that date-of-death market value is the basis, unless the personal representative elects the alternate valuation date. An heir who gets a Schedule A (Form 8971) generally works from the estate tax value shown on it.

The taxable gain is the distance between that starting number and the sale price. Sell close to the date-of-death value and the gain stays modest. Wait while the market climbs and the increase becomes the gain. Arkansas taxes half of a net long-term gain.

Rent or other income the estate collects before closing is a different topic. The state tax agency has a page of fiduciary and estate income tax forms that personal representatives can use.

Using the small estate affidavit

Smaller estates can skip a personal representative. Ark. Code 28-41-101 lets a distributee collect and pass along the assets when property owned at death, less encumbrances, is no more than $100,000. A surviving spouse's or minor children's statutory allowances and the decedent's homestead are left out of the count.

The homestead carve-out is the part that matters with real estate. A family home that was the homestead doesn't eat into the $100,000, although it still gets listed in the affidavit.

  • Wait at least 45 days from the date of death.
  • Make sure no petition to appoint a personal representative is pending or granted.
  • File an affidavit, signed by one or more distributees, with the probate clerk of the circuit court in the proper county.
  • State in it that no claims remain unpaid and that the Department of Human Services either furnished no benefits or was reimbursed.
  • List personal property with values, plus real property by legal description and value, homestead included.
  • Pay the clerk $25 to file and $5 per certified copy. Attaching a will adds no fee.

When the estate holds real property

Thirty days after filing is the deadline for publishing a notice of the death along with the affidavit. From the first publication, creditors have three months to present verified claims, and any that arrive late are barred.

Build your selling timeline around those three months. Buyers and title companies often want to see the filed affidavit, the published notice and a closed claims period before they will accept a deed. The distributee can also open a bank account in the estate's name with no petition or court order, handy for sale proceeds and last bills.

An estate over the limit, or one where heirs disagree, goes to regular administration in the circuit court's probate division. That path has different filings, so ask a probate attorney which applies.

Closing costs and property tax

The state's main closing charge is the real property transfer tax, $3.30 per $1,000 of actual consideration on a deed or instrument conveying realty, for transactions over $100. Ark. Code 26-60-105 breaks that into $1.10 per $1,000 plus a further $2.20 per $1,000 that the purchaser pays.

The county collector takes property tax from the first business day of March through October 15 (Ark. Code 26-36-201). After October 15 the bill is delinquent and a 10% penalty applies. If the estate is still being settled in the fall, check that the current bill hasn't slipped by.

Utilities, insurance and upkeep keep running until the deed is recorded. An empty inherited house can therefore cost money every month even though the estate owes no tax.

First steps for heirs

Sort out who legally owns the house and what paperwork is due, and only then choose between keeping, renting and selling.

  • Find the will, the deed and the newest property tax statement.
  • Call the county assessor or collector about the parcel's tax status.
  • Decide whether the small estate affidavit fits or a personal representative is needed.
  • Get a date-of-death value in writing. It sets the basis for a later sale.
  • Lock the house and keep the insurance active.
  • Talk to a probate attorney and a tax professional before signing a contract.

A short timeline helps. In the first weeks, secure the house and gather papers. At the 45-day mark, a small estate can file its affidavit. Publication follows within 30 days, and then the three-month creditor window runs. Only after that is a clean sale usually possible, unless a personal representative is appointed and handles it another way.

Heirs who live out of state, or who inherited a house needing repairs, sometimes sell for cash to stop the carrying costs and skip the repair projects. A cash buyer closes as-is, and the title company will confirm the estate's papers before the closing date. Ask the title company early what it will need from the estate. Which route suits you depends on the documents and on how soon the family wants this settled.

Frequently asked questions

Is there an Arkansas estate tax?

No. Act 645 of 2003 ended it, and no estate tax return is required for decedents who died after December 31, 2004.

Do heirs owe tax on income the estate earns before the house sells?

That falls outside the estate tax. The Department of Finance and Administration keeps a page of fiduciary and estate income tax forms for personal representatives.

At what size does the federal estate tax apply?

A return is due only if the gross estate, with adjusted taxable gifts and the specific gift tax exemption, tops the filing threshold for the year of death. For 2026 that threshold is $15,000,000.

What is the Arkansas small estate limit?

Property owned at death can total up to $100,000 after encumbrances, not counting the homestead and statutory allowances for a surviving spouse or minor children. Wait at least 45 days after death, and expect a three-month creditor window after the notice is first published.

Will I owe tax if I sell an inherited house right away?

Usually little. Your basis is the date-of-death fair market value, so the gain is the sale price minus that figure, and Arkansas taxes half of a net long-term gain.

Your three routes for removing an occupant

Arkansas offers owners a civil suit named unlawful detainer, a filing under the 2007 residential landlord-tenant statute, and a criminal complaint for refusing to leave. Owners usually pick one of the first two.

Unlawful detainer is defined in Ark. Code § 18-60-304. Holding over once the lease expires qualifies. So does ignoring a written demand to go, skipping rent and then staying put after a three-day written warning, letting the home turn unsafe or unhealthy, or permitting a common nuisance. This is the eviction type owners file most often.

The statutory route begins at § 18-17-901. An owner or agent can go to district court over unpaid rent, an expired occupancy term, or a broken rental agreement. For homes, five days of late rent after the due date works as legal notice that a filing may follow.

Notice periods

The warning an owner must give turns on the reason for ending occupancy. Pick the row that fits your facts and your lease, since the waits are not uniform.

SituationNotice or waiting periodStatute
Rent unpaid, unlawful detainerThree days' written notice to quit§ 18-60-304(3)
Rent unpaid, Landlord-Tenant ActTermination allowed once rent sits unpaid five days past due§ 18-17-701(b)
Other lease violationWritten notice setting an end date no sooner than 14 days after receipt, unless cured§ 18-17-701(a)
Week-to-week tenancyWritten notice at least 7 days ahead of the end date§ 18-17-704(a)
Month-to-month tenancyWritten notice at least 30 days ahead of the end date§ 18-17-704(b)
Criminal failure to vacateTen days' written notice to vacate§ 18-16-101(b)

Boiled down, civil waits start at three days for rent, 14 days for other breaches, and a month for month-to-month occupancy. An owner may also end a tenancy without stating a cause: one rental period of notice ends an oral lease, and a written lease sets its own notice.

Steps once the notice expires

A tenant who is still inside after the deadline leads the owner to file a complaint. Five stages follow.

  • Service. A process server or certified mail has to put the summons and complaint in the tenant's hands.
  • Five days to object. After receiving a summons, the tenant gets five days to file a written objection with the court clerk. Without one, the county sheriff may remove the tenant.
  • Order to vacate or show cause. When the complaint comes with a sworn statement from a person who knows the grounds, the court orders the tenant to leave or to come in and show cause, with ten calendar days running from service. Filing a written answer satisfies the appearance.
  • Hearing. Once the tenant appears, the judge listens to each side. If the tenant prevails, occupancy continues until it ends by agreement or law, rent lapses, or a later eviction case works (§ 18-17-908).
  • Writ of possession. A win for the owner means the clerk issues a writ and the sheriff serves it, which gives the tenant 24 hours to go. Enforcement follows § 18-60-310, as § 18-17-913 directs.

Treat each period as a floor. Hearing dates come from the court calendar, so nothing in the code promises a total timeline from first notice to move-out.

Criminal failure to vacate

A tenant commits a misdemeanor by knowingly staying after receiving ten days' written notice from the owner, an agent or the owner's attorney. See Ark. Code § 18-16-101.

The section adds that a renter who misses rent gives up the right to remain in the dwelling. The fine on conviction runs from $1 to $25 per offense, and every day of deliberate holdover after the notice period ends is a fresh offense.

Can a landlord change the locks or shut off utilities?

No. Only a court order and a sheriff-executed writ of possession can put a tenant out.

  • Swapping the locks counts as a self-help eviction.
  • Hauling out belongings or removing doors and windows counts too.
  • Turning off water, power or other utilities counts as well.

There is one carve-out: those acts may be fine after the tenant has left, or when the owner has a reasonable belief the place is abandoned. A locked-out tenant may sue for forcible entry. The judge can order access restored and award damages, costs and fees. The owner may answer with a counterclaim to evict in the same suit, because a lockout does not create a right to stay where legal grounds for eviction exist.

Property the tenant leaves behind

Once a tenancy is over, by choice or by court order, anything left inside is considered abandoned, and the owner can deal with it however seems best with no claim by the tenant. Items remaining on site also secure a landlord's lien for amounts the tenant promised to pay.

When officers carry out the removal, goods the tenant cannot carry are moved and held at the tenant's cost. A tenant who leaves voluntarily and abandons things lets the owner discard or sell them.

Can a tenant withhold rent over repairs?

No, withholding is not allowed. Section 18-17-502 prevents a tenant from offsetting or holding back rent over a claimed or real shortfall in the implied quality standards. No part of the chapter excuses payment.

For leases signed or renewed after November 1, 2021, the law reads in a baseline: hot and cold running water, electricity, drinkable water, working sewer and plumbing, a sound roof and building envelope, and heating and cooling where the home came with them. A tenant whose unit falls short sends written notice. With rent current and no repair after 30 calendar days, the only remedy is leaving the lease penalty-free and recovering any deposit that can be recovered.

Little Rock layers on its own minimum standards for private rentals holding two or more dwellings. A watertight roof is one. Complaints go to the Department of Housing and Neighborhood Programs, 500 West Markham Street, Suite 120W, phone (501) 371-6825.

What an owner can collect

Under § 18-17-701(c), an owner may collect actual damages, ask for an injunction, and get a judgment or eviction order from circuit or district court with no bond.

Fees for the owner's lawyer are possible if the tenant's nonpayment lacks good faith, and for other willful violations. For a holdover, § 18-17-704 also allows fees where the holdover is in bad faith. A willful violation can add three months of periodic rent or double the actual damages, whichever is larger.

Eviction and selling a rented house

Selling and evicting are separate tracks. The code decides who may possess the house, and a sale does not end a tenancy by itself. Read the lease and speak with an attorney before telling any buyer the house will come vacant.

Some practical links exist. Non-renewal is allowed for any reason except those the Fair Housing Act forbids. Month-to-month tenants are owed 30 days' written notice. You can ask a cash buyer at the outset whether it will accept the house with the tenant in place, which skips the wait for a court date.

Gather these before listing a tenant-occupied house:

  • The lease, any renewal and each notice served.
  • A rent ledger showing paid and late months.
  • Court filings, so the title company can see how a case stands.

The deed brings its own paperwork. State transfer tax runs $3.30 per $1,000 of consideration when the deal exceeds $100, paid through a stamp on the deed. Let the assessor know when an owner-occupied home becomes a rental, since the homestead credit covers a principal residence only.

Frequently asked questions

How long does an Arkansas eviction take?

No law gives a total. Notice ranges from three days to 30 days, the objection window is five days, a show-cause order allows up to ten days to appear, and a writ gives 24 hours. A contested case also waits on a hearing date.

Is eviction a crime in Arkansas?

Only failure to vacate is criminal. Section 18-16-101 makes it a misdemeanor to knowingly stay past a ten-day written notice, with a $1 to $25 fine per offense and a new offense each day.

Can a landlord evict without going to court?

No. A court order comes first and the sheriff executes the writ of possession. Lock changes, door or window removal and utility shutoffs are unlawful self-help unless the tenant is gone or the place seems abandoned.

Does a pending eviction stop me from selling the house?

Nothing bars a sale while a case is open. The lease and the buyer's terms decide the tenant's fate, so have an Arkansas attorney review any contract that promises vacant possession.

Where can a tenant find free legal help with an eviction?

Legal Aid of Arkansas helps qualifying tenants for free at 1-800-952-9243.

What a quitclaim deed does

A quitclaim deed hands over whatever interest the signer holds and promises nothing about its quality. It does not clear a mortgage, a tax lien or a co-owner's share, so it suits people who already trust the title.

Arkansas law is picky about the paper. The conveyance must be acknowledged, the county recorder has to accept the format, and a married owner's homestead pulls the spouse into the signing. Each point gets its own section below.

Format rules the recorder enforces

A recorder can refuse a deed that breaks the format rules in Ark. Code 14-15-402. A missed margin is enough to send a deed back.

  • Paper size is 8.5 by 11 inches.
  • Leave 2.5 inches of blank space at the top right of the first page for the file mark.
  • Sides and bottom need 0.5 inch, and the last page needs 2.5 inches at the bottom.
  • The document carries its title and the names of grantor and grantee.
  • It must be legible and acknowledged under 16-47-207.

The recorder can waive the format for good cause. Documents signed before January 1, 2004, plus plats and surveys, are exempt from the format rules.

Section 14-15-403 adds a second requirement: the preparer's name and address on the first page of any instrument affecting title. If a recorder accepts a noncompliant instrument, the fee is refundable on request within six months, and the instrument still gives notice. Wills, court decrees and instruments signed before August 1, 1959 are exempt.

Does a spouse have to sign a quitclaim on a homestead?

Yes. When the property is the homestead of a married person, the spouse must join in the deed or sign a separate acknowledged deed. Under Ark. Code 18-12-403, an instrument affecting that homestead has no validity without the spouse's participation.

Taxes, laborers' and mechanics' liens, and purchase money are the exceptions. Section 18-12-202 lets a married person acknowledge a conveyance of their own property, or release dower, curtesy or homestead in a spouse's property, as if unmarried, with no separate examination.

A quitclaim signed by one spouse alone can leave a hole in the title. If the house was a homestead, ask the title company whether the other spouse must sign.

Fixing an acknowledgment mistake

Recording cures some acknowledgment defects, but do not plan around that. Section 18-12-208 names defects that will not defeat a recorded instrument.

  • A missing or wrong notary seal, on deeds signed after August 13, 1993.
  • A missing or wrong commission expiration date.
  • A wrong date or a missing county.
  • A notary who moved out of the commissioning county.
  • Wording that departs from the statutory form but makes a good-faith attempt at material compliance.

A defective but recorded deed still gives constructive notice of its contents. For instruments recorded on or after April 8, 2013, a proper jurat can stand in for an acknowledgment certificate.

Recording fees and transfer tax

The circuit clerk, who serves as recorder, charges fees set by statute. Under Ark. Code 21-6-306, Pulaski County charges $15 for the first page of a deed and $5 for each added page. Other counties post their own schedules, so call the clerk where the land sits.

Together the two tax pieces make $3.30 per $1,000 of consideration, and the tax applies only when consideration is over $100. The Miscellaneous Tax Section sells the transfer stamps and answers questions at 501-682-7187.

Quitclaim deeds exempt from transfer tax

Several kinds of transfer are exempt, and a family quitclaim may fit one. Section 26-60-102 lists twelve categories, including these:

  • Property divided between divorcing parties.
  • Instruments given only to secure a debt, and certain transfers to a secured party enforcing a security interest.
  • Corrections of a recorded instrument when tax was already paid.
  • Land sold for delinquent taxes.
  • Beneficiary deeds under 18-12-608.
  • Transfers to or from governments, and some business entity reorganizations.

A FHA, VA or USDA Rural Development home is exempt if the price is $60,000 or less and the seller files a sworn statement that the buyer and spouse have owned no home in the prior three years. A plain gift between relatives is a different matter, so call the state revenue office before assuming an exemption.

Quitclaim or beneficiary deed?

To pass a house at death, a beneficiary deed is often cleaner because it does nothing until the owner dies. Ark. Code 18-12-608 says it must state that it is not effective until death, and it is valid only if recorded with the county recorder before the owner dies.

  • The owner can revoke it any time with a signed, recorded revocation. A will cannot revoke it.
  • If several deeds exist, the last one signed before death controls, whatever the recording order.
  • The transfer stays subject to mortgages, liens and leases that exist at death.
  • For joint tenants or spouses holding by the entirety, all surviving owners must sign.

A beneficiary deed is also exempt from the transfer tax. A quitclaim to a child during life hands over a present interest, so talk to a lawyer before choosing.

Steps for a clean quitclaim

Take the checks in the order the statutes create them, so the recorder has nothing to reject.

  • Confirm every owner and whether the house is a married person's homestead.
  • Put the preparer's name and address on the first page, and leave the file-mark space at the top right.
  • Sign before a notary, with the acknowledgment naming the state and county.
  • Check for a transfer tax exemption, and buy stamps if none applies.
  • Record the deed with the recorder in the county where the property is located, and keep the receipt.

When a quitclaim complicates a sale

A buyer's title company may question the gap a quitclaim leaves. Usual trouble spots are a missing spouse signature, a mortgage still in the old owner's name, and unpaid property tax.

The tax lien binds the house and ranks ahead of other liens under 26-34-101, so a deed between family does not move the tax debt away. If one is already recorded on your house, have the recorded copy and any mortgage statement ready when you call.

Frequently asked questions

Does a quitclaim deed guarantee clear title?

No. It passes only the interest the signer holds and promises nothing about liens, co-owners or defects. A mortgage or tax lien stays on the property after a quitclaim.

Does my spouse have to sign if I quitclaim our home?

Yes, if it is your homestead. Section 18-12-403 voids a homestead instrument unless the spouse joins or signs a separate acknowledged deed, with exceptions for taxes, certain liens and purchase money.

How much does it cost to record a deed in Arkansas?

Pulaski County charges $15 for the first page and $5 for each additional page. Other counties post their own schedules, so ask the circuit clerk in the county where the land is.

What is the Arkansas real estate transfer tax rate?

It is $3.30 per $1,000 of consideration on transfers above $100: $1.10 base plus $2.20 paid by the purchaser. Divorce divisions, security deeds and beneficiary deeds are among the exemptions.

Can I use a quitclaim to transfer a house to my child at death?

A beneficiary deed under 18-12-608 is built for that. It must state that it takes effect at death and be recorded before the owner dies.

What a transfer on death deed is in Arkansas

Arkansas calls it a beneficiary deed. Ark. Code 18-12-608 defines it as a deed, given without current tangible consideration, that conveys an ownership interest to a named grantee when the owner dies. The deed must say in express terms that it does not take effect until that death.

You will hear it called a TOD deed, a transfer on death deed or a beneficiary deed, but all the rules sit in one code section. The legislature built that section in layers: Act 1918 of 2005, Act 243 of 2007 and Act 570 of 2021.

During the owner's life the grantee holds nothing. Subsection (a)(1)(B) says no legal or equitable interest vests in the grantee until the owner dies without having revoked the deed. The owner keeps control of the house, and the person named has no interest to sell, pledge or claim while the owner is alive.

What the deed must contain to be valid

A valid Arkansas beneficiary deed names the grantee, says it takes effect only at death, and is recorded before the owner dies. Recording is the step that most often decides whether the deed works at all.

  • An express statement that the deed has no effect until the owner's death (subsection (a)(1)(A)).
  • A designated grantee, or several, with the form of co-ownership stated.
  • Recording in the county recorder's office of the county where the property sits, before the owner's death. Under (c)(1), a deed not recorded in time is not valid.
  • For property held as tenants by the entirety or as joint tenants with survivorship, a deed designated by all surviving owners that takes effect at the death of the last survivor (b)(1).
  • Substantial compliance with the statutory form (g).

If fewer than all owners sign, subsection (b)(2) makes the deed valid only when the last surviving owner was one of the signers. Subsection (f)(2) separately preserves a deed that is otherwise effective by law and is recorded only after death. That refers to other kinds of deeds, not to a beneficiary deed.

Section 18-12-608 at a glance

Use this map to find the exact statutory language before you rely on any summary, this one included.

(c)Recording before death, and transfers to a trustee
(d)Revocation, and no revocation by will

Who can be named as grantee?

The owner may name one person, several people, a successor or a trustee. The statute is flexible on all four.

  • Several grantees may hold as joint tenants with survivorship, tenants in common, tenants by the entirety, or under any other valid tenancy (a)(2).
  • A successor grantee can be named, including the unnamed heirs of the first grantee, if the deed states the condition that triggers the successor, such as the first grantee not surviving the owner (a)(3).
  • The deed can pass the property to a trustee, including the trustee of a revocable trust, and can name unnamed successor trustees (c)(2).

The tenancy language matters when the house is sold, because a title company will want to know who has to sign. Read it closely before anyone lists the property.

Revoking or replacing a beneficiary deed

An owner may revoke at any time before death by recording a revocation in the same county recorder's office. Subsection (d)(2) requires the revocation to be both signed and recorded while the owner is alive.

Where several owners signed the original deed, any signing owner may revoke. If fewer than all owners sign the revocation, (d)(3) makes it effective only if the last surviving owner signed it and recorded it before that owner's death.

A will cannot undo the deed. Under (d)(4), a compliant beneficiary deed cannot be revoked, altered or amended by the owner's will. When an owner signs more than one beneficiary deed for the same property, subsection (e) gives effect to the one signed last before death, whatever order they were recorded in.

Medicaid recovery against a house passed by beneficiary deed

The state can pursue it. Act 570 of 2021 added language to 18-12-608(a)(1)(B) making the transfer subject to a Department of Human Services claim for reimbursement of federal or state benefits. It also amended section 20-76-436 so the department can claim against the interest a grantee acquires, not only against the estate.

The department's estate recovery rules sort out who is exposed and who is not.

  • People age 55 or older who received long-term care Medicaid in a nursing home or through a home and community-based waiver are covered. Under 55, only people permanently institutionalized.
  • The claim is limited to what Medicaid paid for long-term care, and heirs are not liable above the value of the estate.
  • No claim is made while a surviving spouse is alive, while a child is under 21, or for a blind or disabled child under set conditions.
  • A hardship waiver committee can waive the claim. Factors include whether the home is the sole income-producing asset and whether the home is worth 50 percent or less of the average home price in the county.

Act 570 also gives a grantee a way to ask. When a grantee requests a release or disclaimer in writing, the department has 30 calendar days to assert a claim or provide a disclaimer and release suitable for recording. Where there is no probate, the department sends a demand notice to the county clerk's office and acts if the home is sold.

Other estate steps still apply

The deed moves only the real property it describes. Bank accounts, vehicles and other assets still follow a will, beneficiary designations or the small estate procedure.

For small estates, section 28-41-101 lets a distributee collect and distribute property by affidavit, filed with the probate clerk in the right county. The clerk charges $25 to file and $5 per certified copy. The affidavit must say whether the Department of Human Services provided benefits and, if it did, that the department has been reimbursed.

When the estate includes real property, the distributee publishes notice of the death and the affidavit within 30 days of filing, and creditors then have three months from first publication to present claims. That publication step is one reason families sometimes prefer a recorded beneficiary deed for the house itself.

Selling an inherited Arkansas house as a grantee

A grantee who wants to sell first collects the recorded deed, the owner's death record and any department notice, then finds a buyer and schedules a closing. The sale carries the usual transfer tax: $3.30 per $1,000 of actual consideration on transactions over $100, paid by buying a transfer stamp. The Miscellaneous Tax Section at 501-682-7187 handles corrections to a stamp.

Settle these before listing:

  • Whether any mortgage or lien survives, since the transfer is subject to encumbrances made before or after the deed.
  • Whether the department has sent a claim or a demand notice.
  • Whether the deed named several grantees and how they hold title.
  • Whether the house needs repairs a traditional buyer's lender would require.

A cash buyer can purchase the house as it stands once the title questions are answered, with no lender repair list. This page is general information, so an Arkansas attorney or title company should confirm the steps for your deed.

Frequently asked questions

Does an Arkansas beneficiary deed avoid probate?

It moves the named interest at death under the statute's own terms, so the house does not pass under the owner's will. The transfer is still subject to encumbrances and to a possible Department of Human Services claim, and other assets may still need a probate or small estate step.

When must the deed be recorded?

Before the owner dies. Subsection (c)(1) of 18-12-608 requires recording in the county recorder's office where the property is located, and a deed not recorded in time is not valid.

Can an owner change their mind after recording?

Yes. The owner can record a revocation at any time before death, or sign a newer beneficiary deed. If there are several deeds, the one signed last before death is effective, even if another was recorded later.

Can a will cancel a beneficiary deed?

No. Subsection (d)(4) says a compliant beneficiary deed cannot be revoked, altered or amended by the owner's will.

Does the grantee have to sign or accept the deed?

No acceptance is required by subsections (a) through (h) of 18-12-608. The owner signs and records the deed, and the grantee's interest vests only at the owner's death if the deed has not been revoked.

Which court handles an Arkansas probate?

File in the circuit court of the county where the deceased lived. Under Ark. Code 28-40-102, a nonresident's estate goes to the county holding most of the in-state property by value, and a person who died in Arkansas with no home or property here is handled where the death occurred.

Arkansas has 75 counties, so the clerk you deal with depends on where the owner lived and where the house sits. When cases start in two counties, the later one waits until the circuit court in the first county decides venue. A judge may also move a case before final distribution if it was filed in the wrong county or a transfer helps the estate.

A house in Garland County can belong to an estate opened in Pulaski County. The recorder in the county where the land lies still records the deeds. Probate court and recorder are separate offices, so expect to visit or mail both.

Who can run the estate

First in line is the executor named in the will, then the surviving spouse, then other people who share in the estate. Section 28-48-101 sets that order and attaches short deadlines.

  • A surviving spouse, or the spouse's nominee, petitions within 30 days after the death.
  • Other people entitled to a share, or their nominee, apply within 40 days if there is a spouse and within 30 days if there is none.
  • Any other qualified person may apply after those windows.

Disqualified: anyone under 18, a person of unsound mind, an unpardoned felon, a corporation not authorized to act as a fiduciary in Arkansas, and anyone the court finds unsuitable. A nonresident can serve only if an agent is appointed to accept papers, and the court clerk may be that agent. Heirs who live out of state should sort this out before they plan to serve.

Who owns the house at the moment of death?

With no will, real estate passes to the heirs at once, while personal property goes to the personal representative. Ark. Code 28-9-203 sets that rule and 28-9-206 limits it.

The limits are the surviving spouse's dower or curtesy, homestead rights of the spouse and children, and statutory allowances for a spouse and minor children. A spouse married to the decedent for more than a year can also elect against a will. When there are no descendants the spouse takes the estate, and a marriage of under three years cuts the spouse's share to 50%.

An heir can therefore hold title on paper and still be unable to deliver a clean sale. Buyers, title companies and lenders want to know who the heirs are and whether the court has appointed anyone. Homestead rights of a spouse or child can shrink what an heir is free to sell.

Small estates without a formal case

A distributee, meaning an heir, may collect a small estate by affidavit when no petition for a personal representative is pending, 45 days have gone by, and the net estate is $100,000 or less. The homestead and the spousal and child allowances are left out of that count. The terms are in Ark. Code 28-41-101.

File the affidavit with the probate clerk in the proper county. It gives a legal description and value for any real property, names who lives there, and lists the people entitled to receive it. It also states that no claims are unpaid and that any Department of Human Services benefits were reimbursed. Filing costs $25, each certified copy costs $5, and attaching a will adds nothing.

When real estate is involved, the distributee publishes notice of the death and the filing within 30 days. Creditors then have three months from first publication to present verified claims. Before you rely on an affidavit to sell land, ask the title company whether it will accept that document to move title.

Creditor deadlines

In a formal administration, creditors generally get six months from the first published notice, and Section 28-50-101 bars late claims, with a few timing rules layered on top.

EventTime period
Standard claim deadline6 months after first publication
Copy of notice to known heirs and creditorsWithin 1 month after first publication
Extra time if a creditor is served late30 more days after the period ends
Known creditors who never got noticeBarred 2 years after first publication
Outer limit if no letters or notice5 years after death
Small estate affidavit, real property3 months from first publication

Mortgages and other liens on estate property sit outside the claims deadline. A lender with a mortgage on the house keeps its lien after the six months run, so the payoff comes out of any sale.

Selling estate real estate

When a personal representative sells land, the court order sets the terms and an appraisal comes first. See 28-51-302 and 28-51-303.

  • Three disinterested appraisers who know local values appraise the property under oath. The court may approve a single appraiser if no heir or beneficiary objects.
  • The appraisal is filed with the clerk before the court issues the sale order.
  • The order says whether the sale is private or by auction, and whether it is for cash or on payment terms.
  • A private sale must bring at least the full appraised value. An auction must bring at least three-fourths of it.
  • A sale cannot close more than six months after the order unless a court-ordered reappraisal happened within the 30 days before the sale.

Those floors mean every offer on a probate house gets measured against the appraisal and the hearing schedule, including an as-is cash offer.

How long a will can wait

An application to probate a will must come within five years of the death under Ark. Code 28-40-103. Exceptions cover fraudulent concealment of a will and a nonresident's will already probated elsewhere.

A late probate of a nonresident's will does not harm a buyer who recorded a purchase of Arkansas real property from that estate. Families who leave a house sitting for years should know the clock exists. Waiting also lets taxes, insurance and repair bills pile up on a property nobody has authority over.

Common snags with inherited houses

Typical problems are unclear authority, heirs in several states, a mortgage still in the decedent's name, and a house left empty. Each slows a sale differently.

  • No one has been appointed, so no one can sign for the estate.
  • Heirs disagree about keeping or selling, and all of them hold an interest in real estate that passes at death.
  • Property taxes keep coming, and the tax lien ranks ahead of other liens, so unpaid bills follow the house.
  • A court-approved sale must meet the appraisal floor and wait for a hearing date.

Cash Home Buyers makes as-is offers on inherited houses in Arkansas. Bring the court paperwork you have, and ask an Arkansas probate attorney which route fits your estate.

Frequently asked questions

Do all Arkansas estates have to go through probate?

No. When no petition for a personal representative is pending, 45 days have gone by and the net estate is $100,000 or less (not counting the homestead and family allowances), a distributee can use the small estate affidavit. Larger estates, and estates where authority is disputed, go through the circuit court.

How soon must a spouse ask to be named personal representative?

Within 30 days after the death, if the spouse wants priority over other heirs. Other people entitled to a share apply within 40 days when there is a surviving spouse and within 30 days when there is none, under Ark. Code 28-48-101.

Can heirs sell the house before the estate is closed?

With no will, real estate passes to the heirs at death, but spouse and child homestead rights still apply. Buyers and title companies usually want proof of who has authority, so most sales wait for an appointment or an accepted affidavit.

What price must a probate house bring?

A court-ordered private sale must reach at least the full appraised value, and an auction at least three-fourths of it. The sale cannot close later than six months after the order without a fresh court-ordered appraisal.

Does a mortgage disappear when the owner dies?

No. The claims deadline leaves mortgages and other liens on estate property alone, so the lender keeps its lien and the balance is paid from sale proceeds.

Is your house profit taxed in Arkansas?

Yes, when the federal home sale exclusion doesn't cover it. Arkansas begins with your federal capital gain figures and then applies its own discount, so only part of a long-term gain lands in Arkansas taxable income.

The mechanics live on Form AR1000D. Its core rule is short: 50% of a net long-term capital gain is taxed and the other half is exempt from state tax. You complete the form when you report a gain or loss on federal Schedule D, or a gain on Form 1040 when Schedule D isn't required.

A sale that is fully excluded federally may never reach the form. A sale with a taxable federal gain does, and the Arkansas return picks it up from there.

The federal home sale exclusion

For most sellers, this decides whether any gain is taxed. A seller may exclude up to $250,000 of gain on a main home, or up to $500,000 on a joint return, if both the ownership test and the use test are met (Topic 701 and Publication 523 cover the exceptions).

Both tests look at the five years ending on the sale date. You need at least 24 months of ownership and at least 24 months of living there, and the two periods don't have to be the same stretch of time. On a joint return, either spouse can meet the ownership test, but both must meet the use test. You generally can't use the exclusion if you excluded gain on another home in the two years before this sale.

Reporting is its own duty. If you receive Form 1099-S, you must report the sale even when the gain is excludable. Sellers who can't exclude the whole gain report it on Schedule D and Form 8949.

  • Owned the home at least 24 months of the last 5 years: ownership test met.
  • Lived in it at least 24 months of the last 5 years: use test met.
  • No other home gain excluded in the prior two years: generally required.
  • Gain above $250,000 single or $500,000 joint: the excess is taxable.

The repealed exclusion for sellers over 55

Arkansas once offered a one-time election for sellers who had reached 55: exclude up to $125,000 of home sale gain, or $62,500 on a married separate return, if the home was the principal residence for three of the previous five years. The legislature repealed that election in 1997, so it no longer applies.

The rule text still appears at 26 CAR 100-116, marked repealed, with a note that Acts 1997, No. 328, section 8 removed the statute (Arkansas Code 26-51-305). Older retirement guides may still mention it. Today Arkansas relies on the federal exclusion and the 50% rule.

Arkansas rate and the 50% rule

The top individual income tax rate is 3.9%, cut from 4.4% by the General Assembly and governor in 2024. Half of a net long-term gain is taxed at the ordinary rates.

On the form, a net long-term gain goes on line 7a. Line 7b caps the amount at $10,000,000, and line 8 multiplies the result by 50 percent. That product is your Arkansas taxable amount for long-term gains. Your actual tax depends on total income and the rate schedule that applies to you.

The form also exempts the portion of a net gain above ten million dollars for gains realized on or after January 1, 2014. That threshold is far above any typical house sale.

Type of gain or lossArkansas treatment
Net long-term gain50% taxed
Short-term gainIncluded in full
Net gain above $10,000,000Exempt (gains realized on or after Jan. 1, 2014)
Net capital loss deduction$3,000 ($1,500 per taxpayer for filing status 4 or 5)
Top income tax rate3.9%

Owning less than a year

Short-term gains are taxed differently. The form includes them in full, with no 50% reduction. Anyone who buys a house, fixes it and sells within a year should plan around that.

Losses are limited too. When capital losses exceed gains, you can deduct $3,000 against other income, or $1,500 per taxpayer for filing status 4 or 5. That cap matters most to investors and landlords who sell a rental or a flip at a loss.

Rental and investment houses

Rentals don't get the home sale exclusion unless the owner meets the residence tests, so more of the profit tends to be taxable. Form AR1000D also notes that Arkansas did not adopt the federal bonus depreciation provision from previous years. Depreciation claimed federally can therefore differ from the Arkansas amount, and lines 2, 5 and 10 adjust for the difference.

If you own a rental, work through these steps:

  • Pull the federal depreciation schedule for each year of ownership.
  • Compare it with the amounts allowed on the Arkansas return.
  • Enter any difference on the AR1000D adjustment lines.
  • Confirm the result with a tax professional before filing.

Investors who sell on an installment contract, with part of the price paid in a later year, can use the installment method. The home exclusion stays available even when that method defers some gain.

Inherited houses

Basis usually resets to the home's value on the date the owner died, which often wipes out most of the gain. Publication 551 gives the fair market value at the date of death as the basis for inherited property, or the value on the alternate valuation date if the personal representative chooses it.

That matters to heirs who sell soon after probate. If the house is worth about what it was at death, the taxable gain may be small. If it appreciated afterward, the difference from the date-of-death value is the starting point. Arkansas adds no estate or inheritance tax on top.

Real property transfer tax at closing

The main closing tax is the real property transfer tax. It applies to each deed or instrument conveying realty, at $3.30 per $1,000 of actual consideration on transactions over $100. Ark. Code 26-60-105 splits it into $1.10 per $1,000 under subsection (a) and an additional $2.20 per $1,000 under subsection (b), the latter paid by the purchaser.

The tax is based only on the price paid for land and buildings. Under subsection (c), consideration for tangible or intangible personal property is left out when a conveyance includes both. For stamp questions and corrections, call the Miscellaneous Tax Section at 501-682-7187.

Property tax on the house is a separate bill. Ask the county collector's office for the balance due on the parcel before closing so the title company can pay it from your proceeds.

Frequently asked questions

Does Arkansas have a capital gains tax?

Not a separate one. Gains are part of income tax, but only 50% of a net long-term gain is taxed, and short-term gains are included in full.

Is the sale of my home taxable in Arkansas?

Only if the gain isn't excluded federally. Up to $250,000 of gain on a main home, or $500,000 on a joint return, can be excluded when the ownership and use tests are met. Gain above those amounts flows to your Arkansas return.

Is there still an Arkansas exclusion for homeowners over 55?

No. The one-time $125,000 election in Ark. Code 26-51-305 was repealed by Acts 1997, No. 328, section 8.

What is the top Arkansas income tax rate?

It is 3.9%, down from 4.4% after the 2024 cut.

How much transfer tax is due when I sell?

The state real property transfer tax is $3.30 per $1,000 of consideration on transactions over $100. The additional $2.20 per $1,000 is paid by the purchaser. Form AR1000D is a different matter and covers only the capital gain.
